bio.en: Nicole Forsgren is the leading expert on developer productivity and author of Accelerate, who now researches how AI is changing how engineering teams work.
bio.zh: 妮可·福斯格伦（Nicole Forsgren）是开发者生产力领域的顶尖专家、《Accelerate》一书的作者，如今研究 AI 如何改变工程团队的工作方式。

summary.en: Nicole argues most productivity metrics are a lie - lines of code are trivially gameable and shipping faster only matters if you ship the right thing. She stresses evaluating AI-generated code for reliability, style, and hallucinations rather than accepting it blindly. The episode is a clear-eyed guide to measuring real productivity in the AI era.
summary.zh: 妮可认为，大多数生产力指标都是谎言——代码行数极易被操纵，而"更快交付"只有在交付正确的东西时才有意义。她强调要评估 AI 生成代码的可靠性、风格与是否存在幻觉，而非盲目接受。本期是一份在 AI 时代衡量真实生产力的清醒指南。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of companies are trying to measure productivity for their teams.
turns.zh: 许多公司正试图衡量团队的工作效率。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Most productivity metrics are a lie. If the goal is more lines of code, I can prompt something to write the longest piece of code ever. It's just too easy to gain that system.
turns.zh: 大多数生产力指标都是虚假的。如果目标是写更多代码，我可以让某个工具生成最长的代码片段。想达到这个目标实在太容易了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do I know if my eng team is moving fast enough, if they can move faster, if they're just not performing as well as they can?
turns.zh: 我怎么知道我的工程团队是否进展够快，是否能更快前进，是否只是没有充分发挥他们的潜力？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Most teams can move faster. But faster for what? We can ship trash faster every single day. We need strategy and really smart decisions to know what to ship.
turns.zh: 大多数团队都能更快地推进工作。但更快为了什么？我们每天都能更快地交付糟糕的成果。我们需要战略和明智的决策来决定该交付什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One of the biggest issues we're going to probably have with AI is learning how much to trust code that it generates.
turns.zh: 在人工智能领域，我们可能会面临的最大挑战之一，就是如何判断它生成的代码是否值得信任。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: We can't just put in a command and guess something back and accept it. We really need to evaluate it. Are we seeing hallucinations? What's the reliability? Does it meet the style that we would typically write?
turns.zh: 我们不能只是输入一个命令，然后期待得到一个结果并接受它。我们必须对其进行评估。我们是否产生了幻觉？可靠性如何？它是否符合我们通常的编码风格？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So much of the time is now going to be spent reviewing code versus writing code.
turns.zh: 现在，大量时间将花在代码评审上，而不是写代码。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: There's some real opportunity there to not just rethink workflows, but rethink how we structure our days and how we structure our work. Now, we can also make a 45-minute work block useful because getting into the flow is actually kind of handed off, at least, in part to the machine or the machine can help us get back into the flow by, reminding us of context and generating diagrams of the system.
turns.zh: 这为我们提供了真正的机会，不仅要重新思考工作流程，还要重新思考我们如何安排日常工作和结构化工作。现在，我们还可以让45分钟的工作时间段变得高效，因为进入状态的过程至少部分被机器接管，或者机器可以通过提醒我们上下文和生成系统图来帮助我们重新进入状态。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's just one thing that you think an eng team, a product team can do this week, next week to get more done?
turns.zh: 你认为工程团队或产品团队本周或下周可以做什么来提高效率？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Honestly, I think the best thing you can do-
turns.zh: 说实话，我认为你能做的最好的事情是——

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Thank you. It's so good to be here.
turns.zh: 谢谢。很高兴能来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so good to have you back. I was just watching our first episode, which we did two and a half years ago. I was watching it, and I was both shocked and not shocked that we barely talked about AI. The episode was called How to Measure and Improve Developer Productivity, and we got to AI barely like an hour in and we're just like, "Hmm, I wonder what's going to happen with AI and productivity." Does that just blow your mind?
turns.zh: 很高兴你能回来。我们刚刚回看两年半前录制的第一期节目。看的时候，我既惊讶又不惊讶——我们几乎没怎么谈论AI。那期节目叫《如何衡量和提升开发者生产力》，我们聊到AI的时候已经快一个小时了，大家还只是感叹：“天哪，AI和生产力会碰撞出什么火花呢？”你能想象这有多不可思议吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. Because it was just hitting the scene, it was the topic of so much conversation, and at the same time, so many things don't change. So many things are still important, so many things are the same. Yeah. It's also a little wild that it's been two and a half. Where does time go? Time is a social construct?
turns.zh: 是啊。因为AI当时正风靡一时，大家谈论这个话题的热度很高，但同时很多东西又一如既往。很多东西依然重要，依然没变。是啊，两年半的时间转瞬即逝。时间到底是什么？时间不过是一种社会建构？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Most of our conversation was just questions like, "Well, how might this impact people? How will we change the way we build product?" It was barely a thing back then. Now, it's the only thing that I imagine people want to talk about when they talk about engineering productivity. That's where we're going to be spending a lot of our time focusing on today. The reason I'm excited about this conversation, it feels like there's been so much money poured into AI tools increasing productivity. The fastest growing companies in the world are these engineering AI tools. And now, more and more people are just asking this question of just, "What gains are we getting out of this? How much is this actually helping us be more productive? How do we become more productive?" (00:06:39): You've been at the center of this world for longer than anyone. You've invented so many of the frameworks that people rely on now. So I'm really excited to have you back to talk about this stuff. I want to start with just this term DevEx, it's something that comes up a lot in this whole space, and we're going to hear this term a bunch in this conversation. Can you just explain what is DevEx, this term DevEx?
turns.zh: 是啊。我们那时的讨论大多是诸如“这会对人们产生什么影响？我们会如何改变产品开发方式？”之类的问题。当时AI还只是个新兴概念。如今，谈到工程生产力时，人们谈论的唯一话题就是AI了。这正是我们今天要重点探讨的方向。让我特别兴奋的是，有大量资金投入到提升生产力的AI工具中。全球增长最快的公司正是这些工程AI工具。如今，越来越多人都在追问：我们从中获得了什么收益？AI真正提升了我们的生产力吗？我们该如何提高生产力？（00:06:39）：你比任何人都更深谙这一领域的奥秘。你开发了许多人们如今赖以生存的框架。所以很高兴你能回来谈论这些话题。我想先从DevEx这个术语说起，这个词在整个领域频频出现，在今天的讨论中也会多次出现。你能解释一下DevEx是什么吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: DevEx is developer experience. And when we think about developer experience, we're really talking about what it's like to build software, day to day, for a developer. So the friction that they face, the workflows that they have to go through, any support that they have. It's important because when DevEx is poor, everything else just isn't going to help. The best processes, the best tools, the best... whatever magic you have, if the DevEx is bad, everything kind of takes-
turns.zh: DevEx就是开发者体验。谈到开发者体验，我们实际上是在讨论开发者日常构建软件时的感受——他们面临的阻碍、需要经历的工作流，以及能获得的支持。这很重要，因为当DevEx体验不佳时，其他一切努力都难以奏效。再好的流程、再好的工具，再神奇的魔法，如果DevEx体验不佳，一切都白费了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Within DevEx is productivity, and I think the key insight that you had and other folks in the space of that is not just productivity, but there's also engineering happiness. We're going to get into a lot of these parts, but just maybe speak to... there's productivity and there's broader components to engineers being successful at a company.
turns.zh: DevEx中包含生产力元素，而你和业内其他人提出的关键洞察不仅关乎生产力，还涉及工程师在公司的幸福感。我们会深入探讨这些方面，但或许先谈谈……生产力只是工程师在公司取得成功的更广泛要素之一。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. I love that point because productivity, first of all, is hard to define anyway. But if you're just looking at output, you can get there in a lot of different ways. But if you're getting there in ways that are high toil or high friction, then at some point, a developer is going to burn out. Or if it's super high cognitive load, if it's hard to even think about what you're doing because concentrating on the mechanics of... the plumbing of something, then you don't have the brain space left to come up with really innovative solutions and questions. So I love that it's kind of this self-reinforcing loop in terms of, "You do more work, you do better work." And it's better for people, it's better for the systems, it's better for our customers.
turns.zh: 是的。我很喜欢这一点，因为生产力首先很难定义。但如果你只看产出成果，可以通过多种方式实现。但如果这些方式代价太高，阻碍重重，那么开发者最终会精疲力竭。或者如果认知负荷过高——当你甚至连正在做什么都难以理清，因为得专注于某个技术细节时，就无暇思考创新方案和提出疑问了。所以我很欣赏这种良性循环：你投入更多工作，产出更优质的成果。这对个人、团队和客户都有益处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to get to this later, but I want to actually get to this right now, this idea of flow state for engineers. I was an engineer, actually, early in my career. I went to a school for computer science. I was an engineer for 10 years. The best part of the job for me was just this flow state you enter when you're coding and building, and just things feel like so fun. It feels like AI is making that harder in a lot of ways because there's all these agents you're working with now, there's all this code that's kind of being written for you. Talk about just the importance of flow state to a developer, happiness, developer productivity, and just what you've seen AI impacting. How you've seen AI impacting that?
turns.zh: 我本想稍后再谈这个，但现在就想说说工程师的流畅状态。其实我早年也是工程师，从计算机科学专业毕业后，做了10年工程师。对我而言，工作中最美好的时刻就是进入编码和构建状态时的那种流畅感，一切都变得妙趣横生。遗憾的是，AI在很多方面让这种流畅感变得更难实现了。如今我们要与各种智能助手打交道，有大量代码是为你自动生成的。能否谈谈流畅状态对开发者的意义、对幸福感和生产力的影响，以及AI对此产生的冲击？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Well, there are lots of different ways to talk about DevEx. One way to talk about it is kind of three key things that have components that are important of themselves, and they also kind of reinforce each other. Flow state is one of them, cognitive load is another, and then feedback loops are another. I think when you touch on this... Your question about flow state is a really good one, and I'll admit we're just a few years into this. We're still figuring out what the best flow state and cognitive requirements are for people in this because, to your point, sometimes we're getting interrupted all the time. You don't just get in the flow and lock down, and write a whole bunch of code and do the typing of a whole bunch of code as much anymore. Instead, you're kind of creating a prompt, getting some code back and reviewing the code, trying to integrate what's happening in the system, and that can really interrupt. (00:10:02): At the same time though, it can contribute to flow if... I've seen some senior engineers pull together some tool chains that are really incredible, where they figured out how to keep the flow going. The fast feedback loops really, really work well for them. They can kind of assign out different pieces to agents. It helps them keep in the flow in terms of... Instead of details and line-by-line writing, they're in the flow in terms of, "What's my goal? What are the pieces that I need to get there? How quickly can I get there? So then, I can step back and kind of evaluate everything, and then dive back in and fix some pieces."
turns.zh: DevEx（开发者体验）有多个层面，每个层面都包含关键要素，且相互强化。流畅状态是其中之一，认知负荷是另一个，回馈循环则是另一个维度。我认为你提到的流畅状态问题很切中要害。确实，我们才研究这个领域几年时间，还在摸索最佳的流畅状态和认知要求。比如，有时我们会被各种干扰打断，再也无法沉浸在编码中，快速敲出大量代码的场景越来越少。相反，我们更多是在生成提示、回收代码、审查代码，试图整合系统中的各种变化，而这些干扰确实会破坏流畅状态。（00:10:02）不过同时，回馈循环也能促进流畅状态。我见过一些资深工程师构建出令人惊叹的工具链，他们找到了保持流畅状态的秘诀。快速的反馈循环对他们非常有效。他们能将不同任务分配给智能助手，从而专注于核心目标，快速达成目标。然后退后一步评估，再重新投入优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything more you could say about this engineer that figured out this really cool workflow, about just what that looks like?
turns.zh: 关于那位开发出超酷工作流的工程师，你能否再多讲讲？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I've spoken with a handful of them, and I've kind of watched them work. I haven't built it myself yet. It's on my list. They've been able to set up this really incredible workspace and workflow where... Right now, a lot of us play around with tools and... We'll put in a prompt and we'll get a few lines back or maybe we'll put in a prompt and we'll get whole programs back. Well, what they can do is they can... Many times I'll see them say, to help prime it, "This is what I want to build. It needs to have these basic architectural components. It needs to have this kind of a stack. It needs to follow this general workflow. Help me think that through," and it'll kind of design it for it. And then for each piece, it'll assign an agent to go work on each pace in parallel, and then it'll say and upfront, "These need to be able to work together, make sure it's architected correctly. Make sure we use appropriate APIs and conventions." (00:11:30): Then at the end, they can let it run for a few minutes. They can think through something else that's interesting or they anticipate is going to be hairy, and they come back to something that's probably a little better than vibe coded. Because they were so systematic about it upfront, they're much closer to something that looks like production code.
turns.zh: 我和他们中的几个人聊过，也观察过他们的工作方式。不过我自己还没搭建过相关系统，但这事儿已经列入我的待办清单了。他们成功搭建了一个极其高效的工作环境和流程……目前，我们很多人都在玩转各种工具，有时输入一个提示语，得到几行代码回应，有时输入一个提示语，却得到完整的程序框架。而他们的技术能做到……我经常看到他们这样做：为了让模型更高效地运行，他们会说：“我要搭建这个系统，它需要具备这些基础架构组件，遵循这样的技术栈，遵循这样的工作流程。帮我把这些想清楚。”然后，系统会自动设计出符合这些要求的架构。之后，系统会为每个模块分配一个智能代理，平行处理每个任务阶段，并提前提示：“这些模块必须能够协同工作，确保架构设计合理，使用合适的 API 和约定规范。”（00:11:30）最后，他们只需让系统运行几分钟，就能得到一个比随意编码更优化的成果。因为前期规划得非常系统，最终产出的代码更接近生产环境的标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I'm hearing is spending a little time upfront planning, what all these AI engineers are doing, versus just powering through and just figuring out as you go.
turns.zh: 所以我听下来，关键在于前期花时间规划，这正是这些人工智能工程师们所做的，而不是一味地埋头苦干、边做边调整。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. Let me get to this quite a core question that I think on is a lot of people's minds. A lot of companies are trying to measure productivity for their teams, "Is this improving our productivity? Is this hurting our productivity?" So let me just start with this question, how are people doing this wrong currently when they try to measure their productivity gains with AI?
turns.zh: 好的，不错。让我来谈谈大家最关心的核心问题——很多公司都在试图衡量团队的生产力表现：“这是在提升我们的生产力吗？还是在拖后腿？”那就从这个问题开始吧：当人们试图用人工智能来衡量生产力提升时，现在普遍存在哪些误区？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'll say most productivity metrics are a lie. It's really tricky because, historically... Now, look, lines of code has always been a bad metric, but many folks still use lines of code-
turns.zh: 我得说大多数生产力指标都是虚假的。这确实很棘手，因为从历史上看……现在看来，代码行数一直是个糟糕的衡量标准，但很多人还是在用——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:12:37].

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: ... yeah, as some proxy as some proxy for output or productivity or complexity or something. Well, now, for many of the systems, that they would sometimes whisper and not super talk about that uses lines of code, it's just blown out of the water because, "What do you mean by lines of code?" If the goal is more lines of code, I can prompt something to write the longest piece of code ever and add tons of comments. We know that agents and LLMs tend to be very verbose by definition, and so it's just too easy to gain that system and then introduce complexity and technical debt into all of the work that you're doing. I will say there are some things that we can kind of watch and pay attention to because... So lines of code as a productivity metric isn't great, it's pretty bad. But now, it's kind of more relevant if we can tease out which code came from people and which code came from AI because now we can answer downstream questions. (00:13:40): "What is the code survivability rate? What is the quality of our code? Is our code being fed back into trained systems? And for that code that's retraining systems later, especially if we're doing fine-tuning and local tuning, how much of that is machine generated? What types of loops is that creating, and what types of patterns or biases might it be inadvertently introducing?" On the one hand, it's not good as a productivity metric, but it can be useful. I'll even say the same for DORA. I have done DORA metrics, their speed metrics, their stability metrics. If that's all you're looking at, it's not going to be sufficient anymore because AI has now changed the way we think about feedback loops. They need to be much faster. Now, what DORA's meant for, kind of assessing the pipeline overall in terms of speed and stability. Still, that works. But we can't just blindly apply the existing metrics we've used before because we'll miss super important phenomenon and changes in the way people work.
turns.zh: 嗯，某种代理机制——比如用来提升产出、生产力或复杂度之类的东西。现在，许多系统（他们有时会私下提及但不公开谈论）使用代码行数来衡量，但这完全行不通了，因为人们会问：“代码行数是什么意思？” 如果目标是增加代码行数，我可以编写最长的代码段，还能添加大量注释。我们知道，代理和大语言模型（LLM）天生就很冗长，所以很容易让系统变得复杂，带来技术债务。我得说，有些方面我们可以留意观察，因为……所以用代码行数作为生产力指标并不理想，甚至很糟糕。但现在，如果能区分出哪些代码是人类编写的，哪些是AI生成的，这就更有意义了。这样我们就能回答下游问题了：（00:13:40）“代码的存活率是多少？我们的代码质量如何？这些代码是否被反馈到训练系统中？对于用于重新训练系统的代码，尤其是微调和局部调优后的代码，多少是机器生成的？这会导致哪些循环，又可能无意中引入哪些模式或偏见？” 一方面，作为生产力指标它不理想，但还是有用的。我对DORA也这么看。我做过DORA指标、速度指标、稳定性指标。如果只看这些指标，现在已经不够用了，因为AI改变了我们对反馈循环的看法。反馈循环需要更快。DORA原本用于评估整个管道的速度和稳定性，还是有用的。但我们不能盲目套用以前的指标，否则会错过重要现象和工作方式的变化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. You invented DORA, that was kind of the main framework people used for a long time to measure productivity. And then there's SPACE, there's Core 4, there's probably others. So what I'm hearing here is all these are kind of out of date now, where AI is contributing large portions of code.
turns.zh: 有意思。你发明了DORA，这曾是人们长期用于衡量生产力的主要框架。然后还有SPACE、Core 4，可能还有其他的。所以我听到的意思是，现在这些都过时了，因为AI贡献了大量代码。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I will say if it is a prescriptive metric, it needs to be used only in the way it was prescribed.
turns.zh: 我要说如果这是一个规范性指标，就必须按照规范使用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So
turns.zh: 所以

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: DORA 4, there are four key metrics. There's two speed metrics, deployment frequency and lead time. So code commit to code deploy. There's stability metrics, MTTR and change fail rate. If those are used to assess the speed of the pipeline and the general performance of the pipeline, that's great. If you're trying to use those to understand... Because implied in that is feedback loops, right, because you used to kind of get feedback from customers. But we can't just use that blindly now when we're using AI, as an example, because we have feedback loops much earlier and not even just at the local build and test phase. We have feedback loops throughout, and even sometimes in the middle of some of the pipeline, that we really want to leverage in ways that weren't as useful before. I won't say they weren't possible, but we just didn't really focus there. (00:15:53): So those are prescriptive metrics. When we think about SPACE, SPACE is a framework. It doesn't tell you what metric to use. So I'll say, sometimes people get real frustrated because I didn't tell them what to measure. But now, I think that's the power of it. We're actually seeing that SPACE applies fairly well in these new emerging contexts like AI because we still want to look at... SPACE is an acronym. We still want to look at satisfaction. We still want to look at performance, what's the outcome. We still want to look at activity. Yes, in some ways, lines of code and number of PRs can be useful for something, or number of alerts or number of things, activities or counts. Seize communication and collaboration, this is also super important and useful because it's how our systems communicate with each other, and also how our people do. "What proportion of work is being offloaded to a chat bot versus talking to a senior engineer on the team?" More isn't always better and less isn't always better, it depends. (00:16:50): And then efficiency and flow, "Can people get in the flow? How much time does it take to do things? What is the flow like through our system?" Here, I would probably add a couple of dimensions. So chatting with some of the early authors to say trust. Not to say trust wasn't important before, but now it's very, very front of mind. Right? Before you build your code, if the compile comes back, you're fine. And that's the way it is. LLMs are non-deterministic. Right now, we can't just put in a command and guess something back and accept it. We really need to evaluate it, so, "Are we seeing hallucinations? What's the reliability? Does it meet the style that we would typically write? And if it doesn't meet, is that fine?" So it depends on... Prescriptive. You got to make sure you're using it fit for purpose. Right?
turns.zh: 多拉（DORA）4.0框架有四个关键指标。其中两个是速度指标：部署频率和交付时间，即从代码提交到代码部署的周期。另外还有稳定性指标：平均故障修复时间（MTTR）和变更失败率。如果用这些指标来评估流水线的速度和整体性能，那当然没问题。但如果试图借此理解……因为这背后隐含着反馈循环，对吧？毕竟过去我们是从客户那里获取反馈。但现在使用AI等技术时，我们不能再盲目应用这些方法了，因为反馈循环来得更早，甚至不局限于本地构建和测试阶段，而是贯穿整个流程，有时甚至出现在流水线中间环节。我们需要以更有价值的方式利用这些反馈循环。（00:15:53）：这些是规范性指标。当我们讨论SPACE框架时，SPACE是一个框架，它并不会告诉你该用哪种指标。所以有时人们会感到沮丧，因为我没有告诉他们该衡量什么。但现在，我认为这正是它的价值所在。我们发现SPACE在新兴的AI场景中应用得相当不错，因为我们仍然关注……SPACE是一个缩写。我们仍然关注满意度、性能、结果和活动量。是的，在某些方面，代码行数、PR数量、警报数量等数据可能有用。但抓住沟通与协作也非常重要和有用，因为这关乎我们的系统如何相互通信，以及我们的团队如何协作。“有多少工作是交给聊天机器人完成的，而不是与团队中的高级工程师沟通？”多多并不意味着越多越好，越少越坏，这取决于具体情况。（00:16:50）：然后是效率和流畅性，“人们能否进入流畅状态？完成一项任务需要多长时间？我们的系统流程是怎样的？”在这里，我可能会添加几个维度。与早期的一些作者交流后，我发现信任变得尤为重要。不是说信任以前不重要，而是现在它成了首要考量。对吧？在构建代码之前，如果编译成功，你就觉得没问题。但现在情况不同了。LLM是非确定性的。我们不能只是输入一个命令，然后期待得到一个结果并照单全收。我们真的需要评估它：我们是否看到幻觉了？可靠性如何？它是否符合我们通常的编码风格？如果不符合，那又怎样呢？所以这取决于……规范性指标。你必须确保它们符合实际用途，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We're going to get to your current thinking on the best way to do this stuff. You have a book coming out that explains how to do this well, so we're going to get to that. One thing I wanted to highlight in our last chat that we had, you highlighted that one of the biggest issues we're going to probably have with AI is trust, understanding and learning how much to trust the code that it generates, and also how much... you said this, two and a half years ago, that so much of the time is now going to be spent reviewing code versus writing code. That's exactly what I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 接下来我们要探讨你目前对最佳实践的看法。你即将出版一本书，讲解如何做好这件事。我们接下来就聊聊这个。上次聊天时你提到，AI可能面临的最大挑战之一是信任，理解并学会如何信任它生成的代码，以及如何……你两年半前就提到，现在大部分时间都花在代码评审上而非编写代码上。这正是我听到的反馈。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think it'll be interesting to see how that impacts the way we structure work moving forward. We were talking about flow state and cognitive load. Now that our attention has to focus on things at certain times and it's broken up from how we used to do it, I think there's some real opportunity there to, not just rethink workflows, but rethink how we structure our days and how we structure our work.
turns.zh: 我觉得有趣的是，看看这会如何影响我们未来构建工作的方式。我们之前讨论了心流状态和认知负荷。现在我们的注意力必须在特定时间段内专注于某些事务，而且这种专注方式与过去相比有了很大的不同。我认为这为我们提供了真正的机遇——不仅是重新思考工作流程，更是重新规划我们的一天和工作的结构。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you say more about that? Just what is that? What are you thinking will be happening? Where do you think things go? What are you seeing working?
turns.zh: 你能详细说说吗？这具体指什么？你认为会发生什么？你觉得事情会如何发展？你目前看到哪些有效的做法？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: This is purely speculative. But for example, Gloria Mark has done some really good work on attention and deep work, and humans can get about four hours of good deep work a day. That's about it.
turns.zh: 这纯粹是推测。但比如说，格洛丽亚·马克（Gloria Mark）在注意力和深度工作方面做了非常出色的研究，人类每天能进行约四小时的高效深度工作。仅此而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah,. I feel that.
turns.zh: 是啊，我感同身受。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: That's kind of the upper limit-ish for the most part, and I'm sure people are going to be like, "Well, I am superhuman and I can do-
turns.zh: 这在很大程度上是上限了，我相信人们会想：“嗯，我是超人，能做到——”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What if you take 20 grams of creatine?
turns.zh: 那如果服用20克肌酸呢？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Right. What if we microdose?
turns.zh: 对呀。微剂量呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exact;y.
turns.zh: 没错，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. So in the context of knowing we have about four hours of good deep work... I'm sure many of us have probably hit this, right? We have good periods. Maybe it's morning, maybe it's afternoon for folks. And then you hit a time where you're like, "I'm going to clean up my inbox because that is all I can do right now. I can be functional, but I'm not going to come up with my best innovative, problem solving, authoring, code writing work." A lot of times, the way to do that and to get into it is to have these long chunks to get into flow and to get that deep work. Usually, I'm [inaudible 00:19:43] two hours-ish. An hour can be tricky because it could take time to get into that state. Okay. Well, when we think about what it used to be like, back in the old days, three years ago, three and a half years ago, we could block off four hours of time and we could probably get two or three hours of really good work done. Because we were just focused, right? There were no interruptions, minimal interruptions. (00:20:05): Now, the nature of writing code and systems itself is interrupt driven or full of interruptions, at least, because you start something and then it interjects. So how do we think about that? Does that mean that a four-hour word block is still useful? Probably. But does that mean that now we can also make a 45-minute work block useful? Because getting into the flow is actually kind of handed off, at least, in part to the machine or the machine can help us get back into the flow by reminding us of context and generating diagrams of the system and all the things. So I think that's a really, really interesting area that's just ripe for questions and opportunity. And please, folks, do this research and come back to me because... It might not make my list, but it's such a great question.
turns.zh: 是的。所以在知道我们每天大约有四小时的高效深度工作的前提下……我相信很多人可能都遇到过这种情况，对吧？我们会有高效的工作时段。也许是早上，或者下午。但当你到了某个时候，就会想：“我要清理邮箱了，因为现在我只能做这个。我还能正常工作，但就是无法产出最优质的创新、解决问题、创作或编码成果。” 很多时候，要进入这种状态，获得深度工作，就需要有大块的连续时间。通常，我[00:19:43处语音不清]需要大约两个小时左右。一个小时可能比较困难，因为进入那种状态需要时间。好的。那么回想过去，三年前、三年半前的情况，我们可以划出四小时的专注时间，可能完成两到三个小时的高质量工作。因为那时我们专注度很高，对吧？几乎没有干扰，极少被打断。（00:20:05）现在，编写代码和系统的本质就是被干扰驱动的，或者说充满干扰，至少是这样，因为你刚开始做一件事，就会有其他事情插进来。那么我们该如何看待这种情况？这是否意味着四小时的专注时间仍然有效？很可能。但这是否意味着现在我们也可以让45分钟的专注时间变得有效？因为进入心流状态实际上在某种程度上被交给了机器，或者说机器可以通过提醒我们上下文、生成系统图表等方式帮助我们重新进入心流状态。所以我认为这是一个非常、非常有趣的领域，充满了问题和机遇。请大家做些研究，然后再来找我，因为……它可能不会出现在我的清单上，但这确实是个很棒的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so interesting. Essentially, every engineer is turning into an EM, engineering manager, coordinating all of these junior AI engineers. So your point is even if you have a 30-hour block, you can get deep into code, but you can unblock all these AI engineers that are running off doing tasks. Plus, your point is they remind you of just like, "Here's where you left off. Okay. You can just jump into this code, maybe make some tweaks."
turns.zh: 太有意思了。本质上，每个工程师都在转变为工程经理，协调所有初级AI工程师的工作。所以你的观点是，即便你有30小时的连续工作时间，你也能深入代码，但同时还能帮助那些忙于处理任务的AI工程师解困。此外，你的意思是他们会提醒你：“这里是上次停下的地方。好的，你可以直接接手这段代码，或许再做些微调。”

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Let me zoom out a little bit and... Before we get into your framework for how to approach developer experience, the latest thinking you've got, beyond just obviously engineers doing more is great, what's your best pitch for why companies should really, really focus on developer experience?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。让我稍微退一步讲讲……在我们深入探讨开发者体验框架和最新思路之前——除了让工程师承担更多工作之外，这当然很棒——你能否简要说明为什么公司应该真正重视开发者体验？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I hate to say return of investment, but the business value is... the opportunity here is huge. In general, we write software for fun and for hobbies, but we also have software because it meets a business need. It helps us with market share, it helps us attract and retain customers, it helps us do all of these things. And I think DevEx is important because it enables all of that software creation, it enables all of that problem solving. It enables the super rapid experimentation with customers that... Before, you'd need a while for a prototype and maybe a little bit longer to actually flight it through an A/B test on a production system. You can do it in hours, right now.
turns.zh: 我不想谈论投资回报率，但商业价值……这里蕴藏着巨大机遇。总的来说，我们写软件是为了乐趣和爱好，但软件的存在也是为了满足商业需求。它能助力我们争夺市场份额，吸引并留住客户，完成所有这些任务。我认为开发者体验至关重要，因为它能推动软件的创造，解决问题，让与客户的快速实验成为可能……以前，你需要花很长时间制作原型，或许还要更久才能在生产系统上通过A/B测试验证它。而现在，你可以在数小时内完成这些工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe the opposite end of the spectrum, getting very tactical, before we get into the larger framework, what's just one thing that you think an eng team, a product team can do this week, next week to help their developer experience maybe get more done?
turns.zh: 或许从另一个角度切入，在深入探讨大框架之前，你认为工程团队或产品团队本周、下周可以做些什么来提升开发者体验，完成更多工作？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Honestly, I think the best thing you can do is go talk to people and listen. I love that the audience of this podcast is primarily PMs because they tend to be really good at this. And I would say start with listening and not with tools and automation. So many times companies are like, "Well, I'm just going to build this tool," or, "I'm going to build this thing." Often you build a thing that you yourself have had a challenge with or that is easy to do, easy to automate. And if you just go talk to people and ask the developers like, "Think of yesterday, what did you do yesterday? Walk me through it. What were the points that were just delightful? What were the points that were really difficult? Where did you get frustrated? Where did you get slowed down? Where was there friction?" If you go talk to a handful of people, a lot of times, you can surface a handful of things that are relatively low lift and still have impact or you can identify a process that's unnecessarily complex and slow.
turns.zh: 说实话，我认为最有效的做法就是去倾听和交流。我很高兴这个播客的听众主要是产品经理，因为他们通常很擅长这方面。我建议从倾听开始，而不是先考虑工具和自动化。很多时候，公司会说：“好吧，我要开发这个工具”或者“我要建这个功能”。但往往开发的工具是他们自己曾遇到过挑战的，或者是容易实现、容易自动化的。如果你去和开发者交流，问他们：“回想昨天，昨天都做了什么？带我回顾一下。哪些地方让你感到愉悦？哪些地方特别困难？哪里让你感到沮丧？哪里进展缓慢？哪里存在摩擦？”如果你和几个人交流，通常能发现一些低成本但有影响力的改进，或者识别出一个不必要地复杂和低效的流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the listening to, I hear, almost is you want to help your teams move faster and be happier eng teams. Your advice is just, "Before you do anything, just go ask them what is bothering you."
turns.zh: 所以倾听的要点是，你想帮助团队更高效、更快乐。你的建议就是：“在做任何事情之前，先去问问他们在烦恼什么。”

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Go ask them, yeah. And trust me, most developers are going to be more than happy to tell you what's broken and what's bad. I'll say, there was one company that I had worked with. I remember they had a process that was really difficult and it was on an old mainframe system, and they were going to have to replat the whole thing and so they never went to work on it or talk about it. Everyone hated it because it was this huge delay. I mean, all they had to do was change a process. Sometimes all you have to do is change a process. And they changed it so that instead of... I think someone had to print it out and walk it down three or four flights, and they get approval. And then someone else had to walk it back up, and so it was just that interim. They didn't replat anything. They didn't redesign anything major. They just sent an email.
turns.zh: 去问问他们吧，没错。相信我，大多数开发者都会很乐意告诉你哪里出了问题、哪里做得不好。就拿我曾合作过的一家公司来说吧。我记得他们有一个非常复杂的流程，运行在一台老旧的大型机系统上，本该彻底替换整个系统，但他们始终没去动手改进或讨论这个问题。所有人都对这个流程深恶痛绝，因为它拖延太久了。其实他们只需要改进一个流程就行了。有时候，改进流程就能解决问题。而他们改动后的流程还是沿用了原来的流程——比如，用户需要打印文件、上下楼三四层才能获得审批，再由其他人重新提交流程，整个过程就是在周旋。根本没有彻底替换系统，也没有进行重大设计变更，只是发了封邮件而已。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me push on that and... I'm curious just what are the most common things people do. If you're just starting on, "Okay, we need to focus on engineering experience," what do you find are the most... two or three most common improvements companies need to make?
turns.zh: 让我再深入探讨一下……我很好奇，人们最常做的是哪些改进？如果你刚开始着手“好，我们需要专注于工程经验”，公司最需要改进的三个最常见的问题是什么？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'll say, I'll kind of echo that process, there's almost always a process that can be improved and that can be improved without a lot of engineering lift or a lot of engineering headcount. Most large companies, in particular, have something that is several, several steps. It's the way it is because it's the way it is, but that's no longer the way it is. And even small companies sometimes is just a little too YOLO, and you don't know what it is and you're kind of chasing everyone around. So if you can create a very lightweight process, that can also be helpful. That can be one of the best places to start, especially if you have limited exposure to the whole rest of the org. Sometimes just a team process can help. (00:25:28): I will say from a business leader's standpoint, a lot of what you can do is provide structure and support for this organizational change. Communicate what you're doing, communicate what the priorities are, communicate why this is important, to celebrate wins. Because if folks try to do this, just like a one-off side fully-isolated project, it's really challenging to get some good momentum, to get people to care, and to get them stay involved. Because it feels like it's just another internal project that isn't going to matter or that isn't going to get celebrated, but it has these huge upside potential returns for the business.
turns.zh: 我要说的是流程改进。几乎总有可以优化的地方，而且无需投入大量工程资源或增加工程团队规模。特别是大多数大公司，流程步骤繁琐得令人头疼，但现在情况已然不同。小公司有时也过于随意，方向不明，手忙脚乱。如果能创建一个轻量级的流程，也会很有帮助。这是入手的最佳切入点，尤其是当你对整个组织缺乏全面了解时。团队内部的流程优化也会有所助益。（00:25:28）：从商业领袖的角度来看，你能做的最多就是为组织变革提供框架和支持。清晰传达变革目标、优先事项和意义，及时庆祝成功。若把这项工作当作一次孤立的内部项目，势必难以形成势头，难以激发员工热情，也难以让他们持续参与。员工会觉得这只是又一个无关紧要、无人重视、无法获得认可的内部项目，但它却能为业务带来巨大潜在回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, what I'm hearing here is nothing about tools or technologies. It's not like move to this cloud, it's not like install this new deployment system, it's processes and people and org and morale.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我听到的这些讨论里完全没有提及工具或技术。比如迁移到云平台、安装新的部署系统之类的，全都是流程、人员、组织架构和士气问题。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. Now, there will be technical pieces that are very important, especially now with AI, where we're rethinking how build and test systems work. We're rethinking feedback to users so that it's very, very customized in terms of what is shared and when it is shared. There are a lot of technical pieces that are involved, but that's not the only thing. It's necessary but not sufficient, and that doesn't have to be the place that you start.
turns.zh: 是的。现在确实有一些技术层面的改进很重要，特别是人工智能领域，我们正在重新思考构建和测试系统的机制，重新思考如何根据用户需求提供个性化反馈，调整分享内容和分享时机。技术改进固然重要，但这并非唯一关键点。技术改进是必要条件，但不是充分条件，不必从这里入手。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a hard question I want to ask you that I thought of as you were talking. I feel like this is the question that most founders and heads think about. And the question is just like, how do I know if my eng team is moving fast enough, if they can move faster, if they're just not performing as well as they can? What are just maybe smells, signs that tell you, "Yeah, my team should be moving faster," versus, "This is just the way it works. This is as fast as they can move"?
turns.zh: 我有个难题想问你，这个问题是我在听你讲话时突然想到的。我觉得这是大多数创始人和高管都会思考的问题。问题是，如何判断我的工程团队是否进展足够快，是否能进一步提升效率，以及他们是否没有充分发挥潜力？哪些迹象可能暗示“是时候加快团队节奏了”，又有哪些迹象说明“现状已然如此，团队已经做到极限”？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Most teams can move faster, right? Also, given what we know about cognitive load, not all speed gains are necessarily good. Or the upside is going to be kind of limited once you hit kind of a certain point, and most people are not even near that point. I don't know a single team, frankly. But how do you know? You know if you're always hearing about bills breaking, flaky tests, overly long processes, if you have to request a new system or if you need to provision a new environment, or if it's really, really hard to switch tasks or switch projects. So if someone has an opportunity to go work in another part of an org and they don't for reasons that are unclear, and not political, and anyone says anything about the system, that's usually a pretty good smell that there's friction somewhere. (00:28:20): Because once you finally figure out your system and you're able to get work done, the switching costs can often be really, really high to go anywhere else. So sometimes people will do that. But I've worked with companies where switching orgs within the company, you had to basically pay the same tax as a new hire because the systems were so different and they were so full of friction, and it was so difficult to do so many things.
turns.zh: 大多数团队其实都能提升效率，对吧？不过考虑到认知负荷理论，并非所有速度提升都是有益的。一旦达到某个临界点，效率提升空间就会受限，而大多数团队根本还没触及这个临界点。我真没见过一个团队能完美应对所有挑战。比如系统崩溃、测试不稳定、流程冗长……这些问题都是效率低下的表现。还有，团队需要申请新系统、搭建新环境，或者频繁切换任务或项目时，这些都是效率低下的信号。（00:28:20）一旦团队终于理顺了系统流程，想要跳槽到其他部门却因种种原因受阻——比如政治因素或系统不兼容——这往往就是摩擦的明显信号。毕竟，彻底熟悉现有系统后再跳槽，成本可能极高。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the first part of your answer especially, which is you can always move faster. I think every founder is going to love hearing that. To your point though, there's diminishing returns over time?
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢你回答中的第一部分，即团队永远可以提升效率。我觉得每个创始人都爱听这个。但你也提到，效率提升会有边际效益递减的问题？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. And you don't know about the quality, right? So I think that's the other side is that you can always move faster, but faster for what? Are we making the right business decisions? And I think that's especially where PMs come in. We can ship trash faster every single day. We need strategy and really smart decisions to know what to ship, what to experiment with, what features we want to do in what order and what rollout. The strategy is the core piece, and then think about speeding that up. If we don't have the other pieces in place, I mean, garbage in, garbage out.
turns.zh: 是的。而且效率提升的质量无法保证，对吧？所以另一方面，团队可以提升效率，但提升到什么程度呢？我们是否做出了正确的商业决策？我觉得这正是产品经理的核心职责所在。我们可以每天快速上线垃圾产品，但策略和明智决策才是关键：要知道上线什么、如何实验、按什么顺序推进功能、如何推广。策略是核心，再考虑如何加速执行。如果其他环节不到位，那就是垃圾进垃圾出。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow that thread, but before I do that, just to mirror back what you shared. So signs that your team... There's a lot of low-hanging fruit to improve the productivity of your team as builds are always breaking. There's flaky tests are constantly incorrect, false positives. It's hard to context switch between different projects. You just hear people talking about the system, it's just really hard to work with. Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 我想继续探讨这个话题，但先回顾一下你提到的关键点。比如团队效率低下的迹象……比如系统频繁崩溃、测试不稳定、误报不断、项目切换困难……还有大家抱怨系统难用，这些都是典型症状，对吧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool, okay. So going back to the point you just made, there's a sense that AI is making teams so much faster because it's writing all this code for them. You're going to have all these asynchronous agents, engineers working for you. It feels like a core part of your message is that's just a one part of engineering work and there's so much more, including figuring out what to build... an alignment internally. Maybe just speak to just... There is a lot of opportunity to improve engineering performance productivity, but there's so many other elements that are not improved through AI?
turns.zh: 好的，回到你刚才提到的观点，有一种感觉是人工智能让团队工作速度大大提升，因为它能为他们编写所有代码。未来你将拥有大量异步智能体，工程师为你效力。似乎你的核心观点是，这只是工程工作的一部分，还有更多需要关注的方面，比如确定开发方向、内部协调等。或许你可以再详细讲讲，虽然利用人工智能能提升工程效率，但还有许多其他方面尚未得到优化？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yes. Or could be in the future, right?
turns.zh: 是的，或者说未来可能会实现吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think there are a lot of ways that we can pull in AI tools to help us refine our strategy, refine our message, think about the experimentation methods or targets of experimentation, or think about our total addressable market, but we need to have that strategy and plan fairly well aligned or at least have two or three alternatives that you want to test. Because now, the engineering can go, or at least the prototyping especially, much, much faster. We can throw out prototypes. We can run any tests and experiments that are customer facing, assuming that we have the infrastructure in place, which allows us to learn and progress much faster before. In some places, it used to take months to get something through production to do A/B testing and get feedback. We can do this in a day or two, definitely under a week. But we want to make sure that we're building and testing the right things, "Are we partnering with the right... Do we have the data that we need?" (00:31:24): And I will say AI can actually be a pretty good partner there if you have a good conversation with it, and then also check with you experts, "What type of data should I be looking at? What type of instrumentation do I need? What type of analysis can I do?" Because then, you can also go to your data science team and say, "I'm planning on doing this. I'd like to..." Let's not just YOLO A/B tests because that can be... It's a shame to do a large test and end up disrupting users or disrupting customers, or breaking privacy or security protocols and also end up with data that's unusable because you just can't get the signal that you're looking for. But now, I'm also seeing people kind of accelerate that into a few days versus a few weeks. So they can start those key stakeholder discussions from a much more informed kind of filled out space.
turns.zh: 我认为我们可以通过多种方式引入人工智能工具来优化策略、明确信息重点、规划实验方法或实验目标，或评估潜在市场。但前提是我们必须先制定好清晰的策略和计划，至少准备好两到三种可供测试的备选方案。因为现在工程团队（尤其是原型开发阶段）可以大幅提升效率，我们可以快速迭代原型，开展面向用户的测试实验（前提是具备完善的基础设施支持）。过去可能需要数月才能完成产品上线并进行A/B测试，而现在只需一两天，最多一周即可。但我们需要确保开发和测试的是正确的方向：“我们是否与合适的合作伙伴合作？我们是否拥有所需的数据？”（00:31:24）这里我要说，如果你能与人工智能进行有效对话，再结合专家意见，比如“我需要分析哪些数据？需要哪些监测工具？能进行哪些分析？”，那么人工智能确实能成为很好的合作伙伴。这样一来，我们就能与数据科学团队沟通：“我计划开展这个项目，希望得到你们的支持...” 切勿盲目开展A/B测试，否则可能会扰乱用户体验、违反隐私或安全协议，最终导致数据无用。这方面我也看到，许多团队能将测试周期从数周缩短至数天，从而在更充分的信息基础上开展关键利益相关者讨论。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'd say it's real, and I would also say we don't have great measures for it yet. We're still trying to figure out what to measure and what that looks like. One of the best is going to be velocity, all the way through the system, how quickly can you get a feature or a product or something through the system so that you can then experiment a test, either from idea to final end or even kind of a feature and a piece through the system so we can test. That's really good. Now, that's also hard to tie back directly to a particular AI tool in the hands of a particular developer. But there are some other things that we can look at and we can see, and that I've seen is, again, this kind of rapid prototyping. (00:34:36): I hate lines of code, but I'm going to use the lines of code. We do see... I know I worked with some folks who had kind of a whole set of companies they were looking at, and they found that AI was generating significantly more code for the people who were using it regularly.
