turns.zh:
我认为这是真实的，但目前我们还没有很好的衡量标准。我们仍在探索该如何衡量，以及具体指标应该是什么。其中最有效的指标之一是系统整体的运转速度，即从构思到最终测试的整个过程能多快完成。比如从构思到最终测试，或者从某个功能的开发到测试阶段，这对我们来说都非常有意义。  
（00:34:36）：我讨厌写代码，但还是得用代码。我们确实发现……我认识一些团队，他们研究了多个公司，发现经常使用AI的开发者生成的代码量明显更大。但同时，他们还发现，那些频繁使用AI开发环境（ADE）的开发者，AI工具给他们的代码量也更多。而工程师自己生成的代码量是AI代码生成量的两倍。所以，我认为AI能解锁你的潜力，加速你的工作进程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I've seen people on Twitter sharing is how good OpenAI Codex, especially, is at finding really gnarly bugs. And I think it was Karpathy that shared it. He was so stuck on a bug and, no AI tool could figure it out. And then the latest version of Codex spent an hour or something, looking into it, and found it for him.
turns.zh: 我在推特上看到有人分享OpenAI Codex在查找棘手漏洞方面表现出色，尤其是这个功能。分享这条消息的是Karpathy。他曾深陷一个漏洞困境，所有AI工具都无计可施。最新版的Codex花了一个小时左右进行分析，最终成功帮他找到了问题。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. I'm hearing incredible things like that, right? Well, and even also writing unit tests and spinning up unit tests, and creating documentation and cleaning up documentation because I know now people are like, "Oh. Well, we have agents. I don't need to read the docs because there's the code there." It turns out, agents rely on good data because it's all about how they've been trained or how they've been grounded. And better data gives you better outcomes, and some of that data includes documentation and comments. The better documentation and the better comments you have, the better performance you're going to get out of your AI tools.
turns.zh: 是啊，我也听过很多这样的神奇案例。比如，写单元测试、搭建单元测试环境、编写文档、清理文档等工作。现在人们常说：“哦，有了智能助手，我就不用读文档了，代码里有说明。”但实际上智能助手依赖高质量的数据——这关乎它们的训练质量和约束机制。更好的数据能带来更优的结果，而这些数据就包括文档和注释。文档和注释做得越好，AI工具就能发挥出越好的性能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And AI can help you write that documentation. I've been working with Devin a little bit, and it's really good at that stuff.
turns.zh: 而且AI还能帮你编写这些文档。我和Devin合作过，他在这方面做得很棒。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Let's talk about this framework, this book. So you're publishing a book called Frictionless, which sounds like a dream, "How do you create a dev team that's frictionless?" It's called Frictionless: 7 Steps to Remove Barriers, Unlock Value, and Outpace Your Competition in the Age of AI. There's a seven-step process to this. Walk us through this and maybe give us just context on this book, who it's meant for, what problem it solves, and then the seven steps.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来聊聊这本书。你的新书叫《无摩擦》，这听起来很理想化——“如何打造无摩擦的开发团队？”书名是《无摩擦：在AI时代消除障碍、释放价值、超越竞争的七步指南》。书中提到了七个步骤。能给我们简单介绍一下这本书吗？它面向哪些读者？解决什么问题？然后是七个步骤。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I will say, I also wrote this with Abi Noda who has just... of DX. He has incredible experience in the space. He's worked with hundreds of companies and so it was kind of nice bouncing ideas off of him. Also, thanks to all of the engineering leads and DevEx leads, and CTOs, and engineers that we talked to to make sure that our smells were right. So who is this book for-
turns.zh: 我要说的是，我和Abi Noda共同完成了这本书。他在开发者体验领域经验丰富，曾与数百家公司合作。和他交流想法非常有益。还要感谢所有工程负责人和开发者体验负责人、首席技术官以及工程师们，他们帮助我们确保书中观点准确无误。那么这本书面向谁？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me take a tangent on Abi, and DX, since you mentioned him. This is super interesting, and I think it connects so directly with this conversation. Abi started this company called DX, which is such a great name for a company around developer experience. They just sold the company for a billion dollars to Atlassian. It's a very high multiple on their ARR. It, to me, shows exactly why this conversation is so valuable, just how much value companies are putting into improving developer experience. Atlassian would spend a billion dollars on this. It's an early stage-ish startup. It was doing really well and people loved it, but it was like early stage-ish, a billion dollars. And the idea is they have all these companies working using Jira and all their products. They're all trying to figure out how do we measure productivity. It's worth a lot of money to them. And I know you were an early advisor to them too, so-
turns.zh: 让我顺便谈谈Abi和DX，因为你提到了他。这非常有趣，我觉得这和我们的讨论直接相关。Abi创立了DX公司，这个名字在开发者体验领域堪称绝妙。他们刚刚以10亿美元的价格将公司卖给Atlassian。相较于其年营收（ARR），价格溢价极高。这让我深刻体会到开发者体验为何如此重要，企业对提升开发者体验的重视程度之高令人惊叹。Atlassian愿意为此投入10亿美元。这是一家初创公司，发展势头良好，广受欢迎，但估值却如此之高。其核心理念是，Atlassian旗下所有使用Jira及相关产品的团队都在探索如何衡量生产力。这对他们来说价值非凡。我知道你也是他们的早期顾问之一，所以——

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... it just shows us how important this is.
turns.zh: ……这恰恰说明了这一点的重大意义。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. Well, I think it also shows us how much value you can get out of this. There's so much low-hanging fruit, there's so much unlocked potential, and it's hard to know where to start a lot of times even in... I've been at large companies that have a lot of expertise and a lot of really, really smart people. But if you haven't kind of been in this space and thinking about it this way, it's hard to know where to start or it's easy to make simple mistakes up front that mean you kind of need to start over later. So I guess it also brings us back to, "Who is this book for?" It's for anyone that cares about DevEx, so definitely technology leaders, anyone who's trying to kick off a DevEx program, or is working on a DevEx DevEx improvement program. I think it's particularly relevant for PMs because if you're PMing something that involves software building and creating software, improving DevEx will only help your team. And also, you have key skills and insights and instincts that are so important to DevEx that many times, I will say, I've seen engineering teams just miss.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这也向我们展示了你能从中获得多大的价值。其实有很多显而易见的改进空间，蕴藏着巨大的潜力，但很多时候人们甚至不知道从哪里入手……我曾在大型公司工作过，那里有很多专业知识和非常聪明的人。但如果你没有涉足过这个领域，或者没有用这种思维方式去思考，就很难找到切入点，甚至很容易一开始就犯下低级错误，导致后来不得不从头再来。所以这也让我们回到了一个问题：“这本书适合谁？”它适合任何关心开发者体验（DevEx）的人——尤其是技术领导者、试图启动DevEx项目的人，或者正在推进DevEx改进计划的人。我认为它对产品经理尤其相关，因为如果你负责的项目涉及软件开发和构建，提升DevEx只会让你的团队受益。此外，产品经理拥有对DevEx至关重要的关键技能、洞察力和直觉，但很多时候我发现工程团队会忽视这些关键因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What's the framework? What are the steps? Where do people start?
turns.zh: 好的。框架是什么？步骤是什么？人们应该从哪里开始？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: The book goes through a seven-step process, and then also kind of provides some key kind of principles at the end. Step one is to start the journey. So assuming you're kicking off, you can start the journey. And this involves what we have already talked about. Go talk to people, have a listening tour, synthesize what you learn, visualize the workflow and tools, get a handle on what the current state is. Step two is to get a quick win. So start small, get a quick win, pick the right projects, share out what you've done. Step three is using data to optimize the work. So establish some of your data foundation, find the data that's there, start collecting new data, use some surveys for some really fast insights and may include example surveys. Step four then is to decide strategy and priority. Once you have some data, then you need to know of all the things that are potentially broken. And if you've already gotten your quick win of all the things that are left, "What should I do next?" So we walk through some evaluation frameworks there. (00:40:43): Step five is to sell your strategy. Once you've decided, now you have to kind of convince everyone else. So now you want to get feedback, you want to share why this is the right strategy right now. Step six is to drive change at your scale. So here, we address folks that have local scope of control. If you're starting on just a dev team, you want to do it yourself, kind of grassroots effort or global scope of control. If you're the VP of developer experience or something, there are some things that you can leverage for a top down, and then how do you drive change when you're kind of somewhere in the middle, because you can leverage both types of strategies. And then step seven is to evaluate your progress and show value, and then kind of loop back around. (00:41:27): I will say that we wrote this so that you could kind of jump into any step wherever you are right now. If you're kicking off a team or an initiative, you'll probably want to start at step one. You should definitely start at step one. If you're joining an existing initiative, you could jump into picking the priority or implementing the changes. So those are the seven steps. There's a seven steps, there are a few practices that we also recommend. So thinking about resourcing it, change management, making technology sustainable, and then also bringing a PM lens to this, "How can we think about developer experience as a product, and how do we think about the metrics that we have as a product?"
turns.zh: 整本书共分为七个步骤，最后还总结了一些关键原则。第一步是开启旅程。假设你已经准备就绪，可以开始行动了。这涉及我们之前讨论过的内容：与人交流、开展倾听之旅、整合所获信息、可视化工作流程和工具，并了解当前状况。第二步是快速取得成果。先从小处着手，迅速取得成效，选择合适的项目，并分享成果。第三步是利用数据优化工作。建立数据基础，挖掘现有数据，收集新数据，利用调查快速获取见解，并可能附带示例调查。第四步是确定策略与优先级。一旦掌握数据，就需要了解哪些方面可能存在问题。若你已通过快速成果验证了剩余任务，接下来该如何行动？我们将介绍一些评估框架。（00:40:43）：第五步是推销你的策略。一旦做出决策，就需要说服其他人。你需要收集反馈，解释当前策略的合理性。第六步是在你的层级推动变革。这里针对的是具有本地控制权限的人员。如果你仅从开发团队起步，可以自主推进；若你是开发者体验副总裁等职位，则可以利用自上而下的策略。若你处于中间层级，则可以灵活结合两种策略。第七步是评估进展并展示价值，然后再循环往复。（00:41:27）：我们编写这份内容时，希望读者能根据自身实际情况随时加入任意步骤。若你正组建团队或启动新项目，建议从第一步开始。若你加入现有项目，则可以从确定优先级或实施变革入手。以上就是七个步骤。此外，我们还推荐几项实践：资源配置、变革管理、技术可持续性，以及从产品经理视角思考：如何将开发者体验视为产品，以及如何将现有指标视为产品指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay. I have questions. Point people to the book real quick. What's the URL? How do they get it? When does it come out?
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。我有几个问题。能快速给读者推荐这本书吗？网址是什么？怎么获取？什么时候出版？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, developerexperiencebook.com. Right now, you can sign up for the mailing list. We'll let you know when it's out on pre-order, and we'll also be sharing pieces of the workbook. So we've got almost a hundred page workbook that goes along with the book, and then it should be out by end of year.
turns.zh: 是的，developerexperiencebook.com。目前你可以订阅邮件列表。我们会通知你预售信息，还会分享书中内容。书中附有近百页的工作手册，年底前出版。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So one piece of this is just this term developer experience feels very intentional in that it's not developer productivity, developer work. It's how do we make developer experiences better at our company, which includes they get more done, but also they're happier and things like that. So I think that's an important element of this, right?
turns.zh: 好的。书中提到“开发者体验”这个术语，感觉很用心，它不等同于“开发者生产力”或“开发者工作”，而是强调如何提升公司内开发者的体验，包括提高工作效率、提升幸福感等。我觉得这点很重要，对吧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是的，非常重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Because, again, it's not just about productivity. We talked about this from the frame and the lens of, "We need to be building the right thing." And you want to be productive, but you also want to be thinking about... and this is what engineers are also just really incredibly good at, give them a problem and don't tell them how to solve it, and then they can solve it better. They have the freedom, they have the innovation, they have the creativity so that they can solve this problem. If it's only about productivity, then it's just lines of code or number PRs or whatever. But we really want to talk about value and how do we unlock value, and how do we get value faster. And that involves, yes, making them more productive and removing friction because then, they have the flow and the cognitive load and the things that we kind of talked about.
turns.zh: 因为，再说一次，这不仅仅关乎生产力。我们从“我们需要构建正确的东西”这个框架和视角来探讨这个问题的。你希望提高生产力，但你同时也需要思考……而这正是工程师们非常擅长的地方。给他们一个问题，不要告诉他们如何解决，然后他们就能找到更好的解决方案。他们拥有自由、创新和创造力，从而能够解决这个问题。如果只讲生产力，那就只是写代码、提交 PR 之类的。但我们真正想谈论的是价值，以及如何释放价值，如何更快地获取价值。这就涉及到提高生产力、消除阻碍——这样他们就能顺畅工作，不受认知负荷的困扰，正如我们之前讨论过的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome, okay. And then say someone wants to start this team, what does it usually look like. At Airbnb, I remember this team forming. It was just like an engineer or two, getting it started and taking charge. What do you recommend as the pilot team, and then what does it look like as it grows?
turns.zh: 太棒了，好的。那如果有人想组建这样一个团队，通常会是什么样子呢？在 Airbnb，我记得这个团队的组建过程。最初只有一两名工程师，然后逐渐壮大起来。你建议的试点团队应该是什么样的？随着团队的发展又会如何呢？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: There are a few ways to do this, right? So if you're doing it yourself, you could do it with a couple of engineers, maybe a PM or a PGM or a TPM to kind of help communicate. Because really, comms plans are just so important here. On a small scale, what we want to do is look for those quick wins, look for things that you can do at small scale. Some folks call them things like paper cuts. There small things that you can do to help people see the value and feel the benefit themselves, "How can a developer's work get better? How can their day-to-day work get better? Kind of build momentum from there?" If you're working from a top-down structure and you have the remit, you still want some quick wins, but those quick wins can look a little more global in scale because you have the infrastructure or the backing to make different types of changes that aren't only local. (00:44:56): So an example of a small local change could be just cleaning up your tests, your test suites. Any team could do that, any team could do that. At more global scale, it might be changing organization-wide process that is just overly cumbersome or throwing some resourcing into cleaning up the provisioning environment.
turns.zh: 有几种方法可以做到这一点，对吧？如果你自己组建团队，可以从一两名工程师开始，或许再加上一位产品经理、项目群经理或技术项目经理来协助沟通。因为沟通计划在这里真的非常重要。在小规模阶段，我们要寻找那些快速见效的机会，寻找可以在小规模上实施的措施。有些人把这类措施称为"微调"。就是那些能让人们看到价值、感受到益处的小事情，比如"开发者的工作，日常工作如何能变得更高效？"从这些小胜利中建立起势头。如果你从自上而下的结构出发，并且有授权权限，你仍然需要寻找快速见效的机会，但这些机会可能更具全局性，因为你有基础设施或支持来推动非局部的变革。（00:44:56）：例如，小规模的本地化改进可能只是清理测试代码、测试套件。任何团队都能做到这些。而在更宏观的层面上，可能需要调整整个组织过于繁琐的流程，或者投入资源优化配置环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What kind of impact have you seen from teams like this forming, on the engineering teams at their companies?
turns.zh: 好的。你观察到这类团队的组建对所在公司的工程团队产生了什么样的影响？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'll say I've seen a huge impact for smaller companies, hundreds of thousands of dollars for large companies or in the billions. Well, also, we need to learn how to communicate that, "What does the math look like?" Many times, we can look at saving time, we can look at saving costs, we can look at a lot of different things. We can look at speed to value as speed to market. We can look at risk reduction, but the gains really are there. I will mention that it tends to follow something like the J-curve. So you'll have a couple of quick wins and it'll look like a big win, and then you'll hit kind of a little divot where suddenly the really obvious projects, the low-hanging fruit are handled. So now, we need to do a little bit of work. We might need to build out a little bit more infrastructure. We might need to build out a little more telemetry, so that we can capture the things we want to capture. And then once we get that done, then we start to see those benefits really compound.
turns.zh: 我要说的是，小型公司能感受到巨大的影响，大型公司则能节省数十万美元甚至数十亿美元。当然，我们还需要学会如何传达这些数据：“具体的数据分析结果是怎样的？”很多时候，我们可以从节省时间、降低成本等多个维度去考量。可以从“从速度到价值”到“从速度到市场”，可以从降低风险等角度出发，但实实在在的收益是存在的。我要指出的是，这往往遵循着J曲线模式。最初会有几个快速见效的成果，看起来像是巨大成功，但随后会遇到一个小瓶颈期，原本显而易见的项目、容易实现的目标都已完成。此时，我们就需要付出更多努力，比如完善基础设施、加强遥测系统以收集关键数据。一旦这些工作完成，收益就会呈指数级增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So going back to that measurement number, what do you recommend? How do people find these numbers? Because I think that's so much of the power of this is like, "We saved a million dollars doing this." What do you look at to figure that out?
turns.zh: 回到那个衡量数字，您有什么建议？人们如何获取这些数据？因为我认为这项技术的核心魅力在于：“我们通过这样做节省了100万美元。” 那具体该如何去核算这些收益呢？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think there are a few different things to keep in mind, like who is our key audience, and we usually have a few key audiences. We really want to be able to speak to developers because they're the ones that are going to be using the systems. They'll be partnering with you on either building them or at least providing feedback about what you're doing. So for them, we often want to frame this in terms of things they care about. So time savings. If something gets faster, they can save time. They don't spend time doing setup when they don't need to anymore, related to status reduced toil. So compliance and security are super important. Also, many times it requires several manual steps that... I don't say they're not value add. They're not value add from an individual human perspective. If we can automate as much as possible, that's great, and improved focus time. (00:47:22): That's from the developer side of you. Leadership often cares about... They care about those things, but they often care more about other things. So we could talk about usually costs in dollars, "Can we accelerate revenue? What does our time to value look like? What is our velocity? How quickly can we get feedback from customers?" And for folks and organizations that are in really competitive environments, that can be really compelling because it's all about speed. We could talk about saving money. Here, we can look at maybe quantifying savings. One example is test and build. If we can clean up a test and build suite to a developer, they really want to hear about time saved and more reliable systems. There's less toil because they don't have to keep re-running tests or kind of go clean up test suites. (00:48:13): From the business perspective, cleaning up a test in a build suite can be cloud cost savings because all of those tests are running somewhere on a cloud. And if they always fail or if it's just kind of a waste of spend, that can be useful, recovering some capacity. We can always talk about time and productivity gains, "How much equivalent developer time are we losing on things that are not necessarily value add?" And then sometimes we can correlate to business outcomes and correlate is usually the best we can do here, but there can be some pretty compelling correlations in terms of speeding up time to value and increase market share, for example.
turns.zh: 我认为有几个关键点需要牢记，比如我们的核心受众是谁？通常我们会有几个主要的受众群体。我们非常希望能与开发者有效沟通，因为他们才是实际使用这些系统的群体。他们会与你合作开发系统，或者至少为你的工作提供反馈。因此，对于开发者群体，我们往往需要从他们关心的角度来阐述问题——比如节省时间。如果某项功能能提升效率，他们就能节省时间。无需再重复进行的设置操作，意味着状态维护成本降低。合规性和安全性也至关重要。此外，许多流程往往需要多次手动操作……我并不是说这些操作没有价值，但从个人角度来看，它们并不能算作增值服务。如果能尽可能实现自动化，那当然再好不过，还能提升专注时间。（00:47:22）：这是从开发者角度出发的。而领导层通常更关注……他们当然也会在意这些问题，但他们更关注其他方面。比如成本问题——“我们能否加速营收增长？价值实现周期有多长？开发效率有多高？如何快速获取客户反馈？”对于身处竞争激烈环境的团队和组织来说，这些问题极具吸引力，因为关键在于速度。我们可以谈论节省成本。以测试和构建流程为例，如果能为开发者简化测试和构建套件，他们肯定希望听到节省时间和提升系统可靠性的好消息。这样能减少重复测试或清理测试套件的繁琐工作。（00:48:13）：从商业视角看，清理测试和构建套件还能节省云成本，因为所有测试都在云端运行。如果测试频繁失败或成为资源浪费，那就是双赢的局面——释放了宝贵的计算资源。我们也可以探讨时间和生产力提升——“我们在非增值任务上浪费了多少开发者时间？”有时我们还能将其与商业成果挂钩，比如加快价值实现周期、提升市场份额等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me follow that thread and come back to this, what I think is the biggest question people have right now with AI and productivity, and I don't think anyone has the answer yet, but I'm curious to get your take of just what should people do today? What's the best approach to understanding what impact AI tools are having on their productivity? Because they're spending all this money on there. I don't know, what are we getting out of this? So I guess things are moving faster, but I don't know. So if someone had to just like, "Okay, here's what I should probably try to do," what would be your best advice here for measuring the impact of AI tools on productivity?
turns.zh: 接下来我想延续这个话题，探讨当前人们对AI与生产力关系的最大疑惑。我认为目前还没有人能给出完整答案，但我很想听听你们的看法：当下人们应该如何行动？如何有效评估AI工具对生产力的影响？毕竟大家在AI上投入了大量资金，但成果却不尽如人意。是速度确实加快了，但具体收益如何？如果有人需要一条清晰的路径，如何从AI工具中获取生产力提升的实质性证据？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I would say it depends. In part, it depends on what your leadership chain really cares about. We are usually pretty good at figuring out what matters to developers and we could communicate that to them. But if we're trying to just identify two or three data points to really kind of focus on, because when we're first starting with data, sometimes it can be challenging, what do they care about? Think about the messaging you've been hearing. Have they been talking about market share? Losing market share or competitiveness in the marketplace, if that's it, focus on speed. Think about ways that you can capture metrics for speed from feature to production or feature to customer or feature to experiment and what that feedback loop looks like if they're talking about profit margin all the time. (00:50:18): Now, we always talk about money because this is business. But if that seems to be an overarching narrative, look for ways that you can save money and then translate that into recovered and recouped headcount cost. Or sometimes you'll reinvent, change a process, and then you no longer need as many vendors. So reductions in vendor spent can also help there. I say also it depends because sometimes they'll say something, leadership will say something, and it kind of comes up as a theme. If you could solve a problem that they have or it's something that they're focused on, if you can slightly reframe it even, like if they're calling everything developer productivity, go ahead and call it productivity. If they're calling it velocity, and velocity is what matters to them, think about how to frame this in terms of velocity. If they're talking about transformation or disruption, how does this help with the disruption? Because then, it will resonate with them. We don't want to make them work to understand what it is that we're doing and the value that we provide.
turns.zh: 我觉得这得看情况。在某种程度上，这取决于你的领导层真正关心的内容。我们通常很善于理解开发者关心什么，并能将这些信息传达给他们。但如果我们只是想确定两三个关键数据点来重点关注——毕竟刚开始处理数据时，可能面临挑战——他们关心什么呢？想想你听到的那些反馈。他们一直在谈论市场份额吗？是担心市场份额流失还是竞争力下降？如果是这样，就聚焦于速度。想办法从功能开发到上线、从功能到客户应用、从功能到实验等各个环节捕捉速度指标，以及反馈循环是怎样的。如果他们总在谈论利润率，那就着重节省成本，再转化为人力成本的回收。比如重组流程，减少供应商数量也能节省开支。所以我说这得看情况，因为有时领导会提要求，这些需求会形成一个主旋律。如果你能解决他们的问题，或者聚焦于他们关注的重点，甚至稍作调整——比如他们把一切都归为开发者生产力，那你就沿用这个说法；如果他们强调速度，那就从速度入手；如果他们谈论转型或颠覆，那就从这方面切入，这样才能引起他们的共鸣。我们不想让他们费力去理解我们的工作和我们提供的价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such good advice. Just to reflect back, the advice here is if your company's trying to figure out what sort of impact are AI tools having on our company, first, it's just like, what does the company care about most? What do leaders care about most? Could be market share, could be profit margin, could be velocity. We need higher velocity or we need to transform, transformation. So your advice there is figure that out based on words and phrases you're hearing. Then figure out ways to measure that, ways to measure market share growing, profit margin increasing. I love these examples, like time from feature, idea to production or to experiment, so maybe start tracking that. If it's margin, it's money saved by fewer tests, failing or some vendor you don't have to pay for, things like that. And then velocity, I imagine that's where things like DORA come in of just speed of engineering, shipping, or... What would you think about there for velocity?
turns.zh: 这真是非常好的建议。回想一下，如果你的公司想了解AI工具对公司的影响，首先要明确公司最关注什么？领导最关注什么？可能是市场份额、利润率、速度。我们需要更高的速度或者进行转型。你的建议是根据听到的词汇和短语来判断。比如从功能开发到上线或实验的速度。利润率方面，可以通过减少测试次数、降低供应商成本来节省资金。速度方面，我觉得像DORA这样的工具能帮助衡量工程交付速度、发布速度等指标。你对速度方面有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I would say it's actually one of those... I would pick as broad a swathe as you can. So if you can go from idea to customer or idea to experiment, how long does that take? How long does it typically take, and how long can it take, and does it take now with improved use of AI tooling and reduction in friction? That's where I will say, we talk about this a little bit in the book, how do we deal with attribution challenges? What was responsible for this? Was it the DevEx or was it AI? Go ahead and disclose that. Say, "Yes, we rolled out AI tools. We also had this effort in DevEx. They partnered very closely together." Both of them probably contributed to this, right? If we had AI tools without the DevEx improvements, we probably would've had some improvements, but not nearly as much.
turns.zh: 我想说，这实际上是其中之一……你要尽可能广泛地收集信息。那么，从构思到接触客户，或者从构思到进行实验，这需要多长时间？通常需要多长时间，又可能需要多久？如今借助人工智能工具的改进和流程阻碍的减少，情况又如何呢？关于这一点，我们在书中也稍作探讨——如何应对归因挑战？是什么因素导致了问题的发生？是开发者体验（DevEx）起作用，还是人工智能（AI）？应该公开说明情况。比如说：“是的，我们推出了AI工具，同时也开展了DevEx项目，两者紧密协作。”两者可能都对结果有所贡献，对吧？如果没有AI工具而仅有DevEx改进，我们或许也能取得一定成效，但效果远不及现在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If people were starting to do this today, say they're just like, "I want to start measuring developer experience," are there a two or three metrics everybody basically needs they should just start measuring ASAP?
turns.zh: 如果人们今天才开始做这件事，比如他们只是想：“我要开始衡量开发者体验了”，是否有两三项基本必需的指标，他们应该尽快开始衡量？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: If you're just starting today and if you have nothing at all, talk to people, obviously. After that, I would do surveys because surveys can give you a nice overall view of the landscape quickly so that you know where the big kind of challenges are. I say that because if you're just starting, you might not have instrumentation through your system, all the metrics. And if you do already, it might not be what you think you want. Metrics that were designed without purpose, questionable. Metrics that were designed for another purpose, they might work for what you want, but they might not, so we can't just assume we have them. That's one reason I like surveys, and we include an example in the book. You can just ask a few questions, "How satisfied are you? What are the biggest barriers to your productivity, or what are the biggest challenges to getting work done?" and let them pick either from a set of tools or maybe a set of processes and then say... Let them pick three, just three. (00:54:12): Of those three, how often does this affect you? Is this hourly? Is this daily? Is this weekly? Is this quarterly? Because sometimes it hits you every single day, and you're just mad about it. Sometimes it only hits you once a quarter because it's end of quarter, but it's so onerous, and then kind of open text, like, "Is there anything else we should know?" That can give you incredible signal because by making folks prioritize the top three things... Let them pick everything, it makes the data super, super messy. But three things and how often, you can just come up with a score or a weighted score if you want, and then go kind of dig into, where should that data be? What data do we need? But also, then you've got at least some kind of baseline. It'll be a subjective baseline, but now you'll know what the biggest challenges are.
turns.zh: 如果你是今天才刚开始，没有任何基础，那显然要先和相关人员沟通。之后，可以进行调查，因为调查能快速让你全面了解现状，这样你就能知道主要挑战在哪里。我这么说是因为如果你刚起步，可能系统里没有任何监测工具，所有指标都缺失。即使已有工具，也未必符合你的需求。没有明确目的设计的指标，可能存在疑问。为其他目的设计的指标，或许能满足你的需求，但也未必如此，所以不能想当然地认为现有指标就合适。这就是我喜欢调查的原因，我们在书中也举了例子。你只需问几个问题：“你对现状满意吗？提高生产力的最大障碍是什么？完成工作的主要挑战是什么？” 然后让他们从一系列工具或流程中进行选择，再让他们选三个。（00:54:12）：在这三个问题中，问题频率如何？是每小时一次？每日一次？每周一次？还是每季度一次？因为有时问题每天困扰你，让你暴跳如雷；有时则因季度末而每季度出现一次，但这种繁琐的工作实在令人头疼。然后可以开放式提问，比如：“还有什么我们应该了解的吗？” 这能提供极有价值的信息，因为让人们优先处理前三项问题……如果让他们全选，数据会极其混乱。但选出三个问题并明确频率，你就可以计算得分或加权得分，然后深入研究数据应存储在何处，我们需要哪些数据。同时，至少能获得一个主观基准。尽管是主观基准，但至少能让你了解主要挑战所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how all this just comes back just starting by talking to people and asking them these things, which is very similar to product management and just building great products is, have you talked to your customers? Everyone thinks they're doing this, but most people are not doing this enough.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这一切都始于与人交流并询问他们这些问题，这和产品管理以及打造优质产品非常相似——你和客户交流了吗？每个人都觉得自己在做这件事，但大多数人做得还不够。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: And I will say one thing that's challenging when you think about getting data, so interviews are data and that's important, surveys are a little more quantified because we can turn it into counts, but that's where we also want to be careful. A lot of folks go to write a survey question and they'll say something like, "Were the build and test system slow or complicated in the last week?" You're asking four different questions there. If someone answers yes, was it the build? Was it the test? Was it slow or was it flaky or complicated or something? So it can be really difficult to untangle what the signal is you're actually getting there, and so it is worth the time chatting with someone who's familiar with survey design, having a conversation with Claude or Gemini or ChatGPT around, "Here are the survey questions. Or can you propose some?" And then make sure you take a couple of rounds. Is this a good survey question? What questions can I answer from the data that I get? What problems could I solve? If you can't answer a question with data, don't get it.
turns.zh: 接下来我想说的是，在获取数据方面存在一个挑战。访谈本身就是数据，这很重要；而调查问卷则更具量化性质，因为我们可以将其转化为计数数据，但这时候我们也需要谨慎。很多人在设计调查问卷时，会写类似这样的问题：“过去一周，构建和测试系统是否缓慢或复杂？”但这其实包含了四个不同的问题。如果有人回答“是”，他们指的是构建环节？测试环节？还是系统缓慢、故障频出、流程复杂？因此，要想理清所获取的数据传递的真实信息，往往需要花费大量时间。为此，与熟悉调查设计的人交流非常重要，比如和Claude、Gemini或ChatGPT讨论：“这些是调查问卷的问题。或者你能给些建议吗？”并确保反复校对：这个问题是否合适？我能从收集的数据中解答哪些问题？又能解决哪些难题？如果某个问题无法用数据解答，那就别收集了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you have example surveys in your book for folks that want to just copy and paste and not have to think about this much.
turns.zh: 你的书中还提供了示例调查问卷，方便读者直接复制使用，无需过多思考。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, example surveys, a lot of example questions. We even recommend what the format, what the flow should look like, how long it should be, how long it should not be.
turns.zh: 是的，有很多示例调查问卷。我们甚至会建议问卷的格式、流程、时长等细节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One thing that I was reading is that you don't love happiness surveys specifically, asking engineers how happy they are, is that true? If so, why is that?
turns.zh: 我曾读到你不喜欢专门针对工程师幸福感的调查问卷，是这样吗？如果是，为什么？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I don't, no. Well, I'll say I don't love a happiness survey because there are too many things that contribute to happiness. Happiness is a lot, right? So happiness is work, happiness is family, happiness is hobbies, happiness is weekends, happiness... There are so many things that contribute to happiness. Now, that doesn't mean I don't care about happiness. I think happiness surveys are not particularly useful here. What can be helpful is satisfaction and people are like, "That's the same thing." It's not because you can ask, "Are you satisfied with this tool?" and then ask some follow-up questions. Now, those two are related because the more satisfied you are with your job and your tools and the work and your team, it contributes to happiness. I used to joke... Remember the golf commercials like, "Happy cows like happy cheese"?
turns.zh: 确实不喜欢。幸福感的来源太多，幸福本身是个复杂的概念。工作、家庭、爱好、周末……太多因素影响着幸福感。不过这并不意味着我不关注幸福感。我认为幸福感调查在这里并不实用，更有价值的是满意度调查。比如问“你对这款工具满意吗？”并追问后续问题。这两者是相关的，因为对工作、工具、团队和合作伙伴越满意，就越有助于提升幸福感。我曾开玩笑说……比如高尔夫广告里的“快乐奶牛产出快乐奶酪”？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I had a Calabrian. That was the best. Happy devs make happy code. They write better programs, they do better work, they're better team members and collaborators. But capturing and trying to directly influence happiness, that's not what we are here for. It's too challenging, it's too all-encompassing. Satisfaction can give us some signal.
turns.zh: 我用过一款叫Calabrian的工具，那是最棒的。快乐的开发者能写出快乐的代码，他们编程更出色，工作更高效，也是更好的团队成员和协作者。但试图直接影响幸福感，这不是我们的目标。它太具挑战性，太宏大了。满意度调查能给我们一些信号。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In a totally different direction, in terms of just tools you see people using, are there any that just like, "Oh, yeah, this one's really commonly great." For people, this is just a tool people are finding a lot of success with. There's the common ones, Copilot, Cursor. I don't know. Is there anything that stands out that you want to share, just like, "Hey, you should check this tool out. People seem to love it"?
turns.zh: 换个完全不同的方向，谈谈你见过的常用工具，有没有那种大家一致认为很棒的？比如Copilot、Cursor之类的，我不知道，还有什么突出的工具值得推荐？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think they're huge, right? Copilot, Cursor, Gemini.
turns.zh: 我觉得它们都非常棒，对吧？Copilot、Cursor、Gemini。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Claude Code.
turns.zh: 克劳德代码。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yep, Claude Code. I love Claude Code.
turns.zh: 是啊，克劳德代码。我超爱克劳德代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a whole post coming on ways to use Claude Code for non-engineering use cases.
turns.zh: 我准备写一篇文章，介绍如何在非工程领域场景中使用克劳德代码。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Cool. Nice.
turns.zh: 太酷了。真不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so interesting. For example, Claude Code, "Find ways to clean up storage on my laptop," and it just tells you there's a bunch of files. It's just like ChatGPT running on your computer and you could do all kinds of crazy stuff on your computer for you, like a mini God.
turns.zh: 这太有趣了。比如说，用克劳德代码回答“如何清理笔记本电脑存储空间”这样的问题，它会直接列出一堆文件。这就好像在你的电脑上运行了ChatGPT一样，你可以让它在你的电脑上做各种疯狂的事，简直就是个小神仙。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'm going to do that now. This is great.
turns.zh: 我现在就去试试看。这太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's so good. Yeah, that's why I'm writing this. I had Dan Shipper was on the podcast and he said Claude Code is the most underrated AI tool out there because people don't realize what it's capable of. It's not just for coding, and that's what I'm trying to explore more and more. Okay. Is there anything else that you think would be valuable to help people improve their developer experience, help them adapt to this new world of AI and engineering that we haven't covered?
turns.zh: 真是太好了。没错，这就是我写这篇文章的原因。我邀请了丹·希珀上播客，他说克劳德代码是目前最被低估的人工智能工具，因为人们没意识到它能做什么。它不只是用于编程，这正是我想不断探索的方向。好的。你觉得还有什么对帮助人们提升开发者体验、适应我们尚未涉及的AI与工程新世界有价值的内容吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think something that's important to think about in general is to bring a product mindset to any type of DevEx improvements that are happening, and also the metrics that we collect and capture. By that, I mean we want to identify a problem, make sure we're solving a problem for a set of users. We want to think about creating MVPs and experiments and get fast feedback, do some rapid iteration. We want to have a strategy. We want to know who our addressable market is. We want to know what success is. We want to basically have a go-to-market function. We need to have comms. We need to get continuous feedback from our customers. We want to keep improving. And, at some point, we want to think about sunsetting something. Is it in maintenance mode? Is it sun setting? (01:00:12): And I think that's important in general, but I think it's extra important now because when we have AI tools, we're using AI tools, we're embedding AI into our products, things are changing so rapidly that it can be really important to take half a beat and say, "Okay, what's the problem I'm trying to solve right here? Is this metric that we've had for the last 10 years still important or should this be sunset because it's not really important anymore? It's not driving the types of decisions and actions that I need."
turns.zh: 我认为总体而言，重要的是要为正在进行的任何开发者体验改进带来产品思维，以及我们收集和捕捉的指标。我的意思是，我们要识别问题，确保为一组用户解决问题。我们要考虑创建最简可行产品和实验，获取快速反馈，进行快速迭代。我们需要有策略。我们需要知道我们的目标市场是谁。我们需要知道成功是什么。我们基本上需要有上市功能。我们需要有沟通。我们需要从客户那里获得持续反馈。我们需要不断改进。在某个时候，我们需要考虑让某个东西退役。它是处于维护模式吗？还是要退役了？（01:00:12）我认为这在总体上很重要，但现在尤为重要，因为当我们使用AI工具，将AI嵌入到我们的产品中时，事情变化太快了。以至于花点时间停下来想一想：“好的，我现在要解决什么问题？我们过去10年一直使用的这个指标还重要吗？还是因为它不再重要而应该退役？它无法驱动我需要的决策和行动了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get to our exciting lightning round, I want to take us to AI Corner, which is a recurring segment on this podcast. Is there some way that you've found a use for an AI tool in your life, in your work that you think might be fun to share, that you think might be useful to other people?
turns.zh: 在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，我想先带大家进入AI角落，这是本播客的固定环节。你有没有在生活或工作中找到过AI工具的用途，你觉得可能很有趣，值得和其他人分享？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I have been working on some home design and redecorating rooms and stuff. I'm working with a designer because I know what I like, but I don't know how to get there, I'm not good at this. But I've really been loving ChatGPT and Gemini especially to render pictures for me, so I can give it the floor plan, I can give it one shot of the room that's definitely not what it's supposed to look like, and then I can give it pictures of a couple different things, and then I can just tell it change the walls or change the furniture layout or change something. It helps me and it's relatively quick. It helps me kind of visualize the things... Again, I know what I like, but I don't know how to get there, so I know if I like it or not, which is probably a very random use, but it's fun for now.
turns.zh: 我一直在做一些家装和房间布置之类的工作。我请了一位设计师帮忙，因为我知道自己喜欢什么样的，但就是不知道怎么实现——我对这方面不太在行。不过我最近特别喜欢用ChatGPT和Gemini来渲染图片。比如，我可以给它提供平面图，展示某个房间的现状照片（肯定不是理想效果），再上传几张不同物品的图片，然后让它调整墙面设计、家具布局等等。这个功能对我帮助很大，而且操作起来相对快捷。它能帮我把想象中的场景具象化……再说，我确实知道自己喜欢什么，但就是不知道怎么实现。所以用它来判断自己喜不喜欢某个方案，可能有点随意，但暂时还挺有趣的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My wife does exactly the same thing. She's sending me constantly, "Here's what this rug will look like in our living room. Here's this water feature." It's so good and it keeps getting better. It's just like, "Wow, that's exactly our house with this new rug," and all you do is just upload these two photos and just like, "Cool. How would this look in our room?"
turns.zh: 我妻子也一直在这么做。她老是发消息给我：“这块地毯放在客厅会是什么样子？” 这个功能越来越好了。比如，我上传两张照片，描述一下场景，它就能生成房间效果图，甚至会加个狗床进去，毕竟我养了狗。我当时就惊叹：“我根本没让它加狗床啊，但这颜色和款式确实是我房间该有的！”

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, I've been impressed a couple times. Definitely the machines are listening to us. It's given me a mock-up of a room or something and then it throws in a dog bed, because I have dogs. I'm like, "I did not tell you to do that, but yeah, that's probably the color and style of dog bed that I should have in this room."
turns.zh: 是啊，有几次体验让我印象深刻。感觉机器真的能理解我们的需求。比如，它会根据已有信息模拟房间效果，还能推荐合适的狗床款式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, have you tried this use case, ask ChatGPT, "Generate an image of what you think my house looks like based on everything you know about me."
turns.zh: 说到这，你有没有试过让ChatGPT根据已有信息生成房子的效果图？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I haven't.
turns.zh: 我还没试过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Because it has memory and it remembers everything you've talked about, and it's hilarious. You got to do it.
turns.zh: 因为它有记忆功能，能记住你之前的对话内容，真的太神了。你一定要试试。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Okay, that's on my to-do list.
turns.zh: 好的，这事儿加到我的待办清单里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There we go. Bonus use case. Nicole, with that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. I've got five questions for you. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，现在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节。我有五个问题要问你，准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Awesome. Let's go.
turns.zh: 太棒了。开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Outlive by Peter Attia is fantastic. Another one that's I guess maybe related, I hurt my back so it's not great, Back Mechanic by Stuart McGill is incredible. Shout out to anyone who has hurt lower back. It's for a lay person to read through and figure out how to fix lower back problems. It's kind of a random one. I will say I love How Big Things Get Done. I can't pronounce the names. I think one's... There's Scandinavian, one is. It kind of dissects really large projects through recent-ish history and where they failed and why. And I think it's really interesting for us to think about, especially now in this AI moment where basically all of our at least software systems are going to be changing. So how do we think about approaching what is essentially going to be a very large project? And then, sorry, I'm going to throw in a bonus one, The Undoing Project by Michael Lewis. Matt Velloso recommended it to me, and it's so good.
turns.zh: 彼得·阿蒂亚的《Outlive》非常棒。还有一本可能相关的书，《Back Mechanic》（背部医生），斯图尔特·麦吉尔写的，写得超棒。对有腰伤的人特别有帮助。这本书适合普通人阅读，教你如何解决下背部问题。有点冷门。不过我得说，我很喜欢《How Big Things Get Done》（大事如何成型）。我念不出书名了。有一本是斯堪的纳维亚相关的，另一本也是。这本书通过近代史上的大型项目案例，剖析它们的成败原因。对我们思考如何应对大型项目很有启发，尤其是现在AI时代，几乎所有软件系统都要升级。那么我们该如何着手处理这类大型项目呢？最后，再推荐一本迈克尔·刘易斯的《The Undoing Project》（破解难题）。马特·维洛索推荐给我的，真的很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, I read that-
turns.zh: 是的，我读过这本书-

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I audibly gasped at the last sentence.
turns.zh: 听到最后那句话时，我忍不住倒吸了一口凉气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh. I was like, "What?"
turns.zh: 哦。我当时就想：“什么？”

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I was [inaudible 01:03:48]. Yeah, I was not expecting it.
turns.zh: 我当时（声音不清，01:34:48）。是啊，我完全没想到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I read that and I do not remember that last sentence. Oh, man. Okay, cool. Next question. Do you have a favorite movie or TV show you recently watched and enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我读到那句话时，完全不记得最后那句话了。天哪。好吧，下一个问题。你最近有没有看过喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I'll say I watch Love Is Blind. If I got to shut down at the end of the day, Love Is Blind is fun.
turns.zh: 我得说我一直在看《爱情盲盒》。要是让我结束一天的工作时放松一下，《爱情盲盒》就很不错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a new season out.
turns.zh: 新一季已经上线了。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, very excited... and Shrinking. Have you seen Shrinking?
turns.zh: 是啊，我特别期待……还有《缩小》。你看过《缩小》吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. I think I started The Therapist and yeah, I gave it a shot.
turns.zh: 没看过。我想我开始看《心理治疗师》了，但没坚持下去。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Strongly recommend it. It's cute.
turns.zh: 强烈推荐。挺可爱的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Is there a product you've recently discovered that you really love? Could be an app, could be some kitchen gadgets, some clothing.
turns.zh: 不错啊。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？可以是应用程序、厨房小工具或者服装之类的。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, the Ninja Creami is-
turns.zh: 是啊，Ninja Creami——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you say this last time?
turns.zh: 你上次也提到过这个？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I don't know. I may have. I don't think so.
turns.zh: 我不确定。我可能说过，但我觉得应该没说过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Somebody said this and I still remember it. It's like-
turns.zh: 有人说过这句话，我至今还记得。就像——

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: It's so good.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... you make ice cream and stuff with it, right?
turns.zh: ……你可以用它来制作冰淇淋之类的，对吧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, and you can basically freeze a protein shake and then it turns it into ice cream-
turns.zh: 对啊，你基本上可以把蛋白质奶昔冷冻起来，然后它就能变成冰淇淋了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man.
turns.zh: 哦，天哪。

turns.en: ... which is delicious. Another one is a Jura coffee maker. I'd love good coffee and I'm not great at making it, so I can just push the button and it'll give me anything I want, including lattes, cappuccinos or anything. So that's kind of fun.
turns.zh: ……味道超棒。另一个是朱拉咖啡机。我喜欢喝好咖啡，但我不太擅长冲泡，所以只要按下按钮，它就能给我调制出任何我想要的咖啡，包括拿铁、卡布奇诺之类的。这还挺有趣的。

turns.en: Sweet, okay. Do you have a favorite-

turns.zh: 就糖和咖啡因吧。我只需要能撑过一天。

turns.zh: 这就是工程生产力101。

turns.zh: 哦，天哪。好的，再问两个问题。你有没有特别喜欢的的人生格言，经常在工作或生活中用到，并以各种方式反复回味的？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, I think one that's come up a couple times, it's not a verbatim thing, I think it's more the vibe, hindsight is 2020, but it's also really dumb. I think if we made the best decision we could at the time with the information that we had available, then it is what it is. If you make a bad decision because you made a bad decision and you knew better, you had the information, not great. I don't think we give ourselves or other people enough grace because we always end up finding more information out later.
turns.zh: 有啊，我觉得有句话出现过好几次，虽然不是原封不动的，但那种感觉很到位。事后看来，一切都已注定，但这话其实挺傻的。我觉得如果我们在当时能根据已有的信息做出最佳决策，那结果就是注定的。但如果你因为明明知道更好却做了错误的决定，那就不太好了。我觉得我们对自己和他人都太苛刻了，因为后来总能找到更多信息。

turns.en: Hear, hear. Final question. I was going to ask you something else, but as we are preparing for this, you shared that you have a new role at Google. Maybe just talk about that, what you're up to there, why you joined Google, anything folks should know.
turns.zh: 说得对。最后一个问题。我本来想问别的，但在准备过程中，你提到你在谷歌有新职位了。能聊聊吗？你在那里做些什么？为什么加入谷歌？有什么值得大家了解的吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Sure. I am senior director of developer intelligence and core developer. It's super exciting and super fun because of all of these things we've been talking about. It's focused on Google and all their properties and their underlying infrastructure, how can we improve developer experience, developer productivity, velocity, all of these things we've been talking about and, because kind of the numbers person, how do we want to think about measuring it, how does measurement change, how do feedback loops change, how can we improve the experience throughout and then kind of drive that change through an organization in ways that are meaningful and impactful and faster than they've been before.
turns.zh: 好的。我是开发者情报与核心开发团队的高级总监。正因为我们刚刚讨论的这些内容，这份工作超级令人兴奋、超级有趣。我们的工作重点是谷歌及其旗下所有产品与底层基础设施，如何提升开发者体验、开发者生产力和开发速度——这些都是我们一直在探讨的核心议题。作为数据分析师，我还需要思考如何衡量这些成果，衡量标准如何调整，反馈循环如何优化，以及如何通过有意义、有效且更高效的方式，在整个组织内推动变革。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Nice job, Google, getting Nicole. What a win. I need to get some more Google stock ASAP. Okay, two follow-up questions. Where can folks find you online and find your book online if they want to dig deeper? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 谷歌能邀请到妮可真是太棒了。真是个大成功。我得赶紧买些谷歌股票了。好的，两个后续问题。听众如果想深入了解，可以在哪里找到你的在线资料和书籍？听众如何能为你提供有用的反馈？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Online, you can find the book at developerexperiencebook.com, I'm at nicolefv.com, and LinkedIn occasionally. Sometimes it's a mess. I try to wade through all of the noise. I get there to be useful, sign up for the book and the workbooks. The workbooks are free. I'd love to get any kind of feedback on what works, what doesn't. I always love hearing those kind of stories.
turns.zh: 在线平台上，大家可以在developerexperiencebook.com找到这本书，我个人主页是nicolefv.com，偶尔也会在LinkedIn上活跃。不过有时内容比较杂乱。我努力过滤掉各种干扰信息，专注于提供有用的内容。欢迎注册获取书籍和配套工作手册。工作手册是免费的。我很期待收到大家的反馈，无论是成功经验还是改进建议。这样的故事总是让我倍感欣慰。

turns.en: Nicole, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 妮可，非常感谢你今天的到来。

turns.en: Thanks for having me, Lenny.
turns.zh: 莱尼，感谢邀请。
